item.title: Peter Obi congratulates Flamingos on U-17 Women’s World Cup triumph
item.description: The Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Peter Obi, has congratulated the Nigeria U-17 women’s national football team, the Flamingos, following their triumph at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco. Obi praised the players for their talent, resilience, hard work and dedication, saying their achievement had brought immense joy and pride to Nigerians. In a congratulatory message posted on his X handle on Saturday, the former Anambra State governor commended the team for representing the country proudly on the international stage. He said the players had earned a special place in the hearts of Nigerians through their outstanding performance. “Thank you for raising our flag high and bringing immense joy to our nation. Your remarkable talent, resilience, hard work and dedication have earned you a special place in the hearts of Nigerians,” Obi said. He added that the team’s accomplishment demonstrated the potential of Nigerian youths and their ability to excel through determination and commitment. “You have made our nation proud, and we truly appreciate your outstanding efforts. Congratulations, champions!” he stated. Obi concluded his message with his familiar expression of optimism about Nigeria’s future, saying, “A new Nigeria is possible.” The post Peter Obi congratulates Flamingos on U-17 Women’s World Cup triumph appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos
item.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru President Bola Tinubu has congratulated Nigeria’s Flamingos for making history as the first African team to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup following their 2-1 victory over Japan in Saturday’s final in Rabat, Morocco. The president, who received the cheering news upon his return from campaign engagements in Akwa Ibom and Rivers States, hailed Nigeria’s maiden triumph as a proud moment for the nation and a landmark achievement for African women’s football. “What wonderful news to return home to! Our young girls have conquered the world and given Nigerians everywhere another reason to celebrate our great country. “To our gallant Flamingos, I say congratulations. You have shown courage, discipline, determination, and the Nigerian spirit of never giving up. “I followed your journey throughout this tournament, and after your semi-final victory, you promised to bring the trophy home. Today, you have kept that promise. You believed in yourselves, fought for one another, and carried our nation’s flag to the very top of the world. “Your victory is an inspiration to millions of young Nigerian girls who dream of achieving greatness. You have shown them that with hard work, opportunity, and determination, they too can reach the highest levels of achievement. “Today, Nigeria celebrates you. You have written your names in gold, and your country is immensely proud of you.” The president particularly applauds Awawu Bashiru and Oluebube Umejiaku, whose goals secured the historic victory, while commending the entire squad for their exceptional teamwork throughout the tournament. He also congratulates the coaching crew, the Nigeria Football Federation, and the National Sports Commission for their contributions to the team’s success. President Tinubu reaffirms his administration’s commitment to investing in grassroots sports development and expanding opportunities for young Nigerians, particularly girls, to discover, nurture, and fulfill their potential. “Congratulations once again, Flamingos. Thank you for making Nigeria proud.” The post U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 68 days to polls: Struggling Nigerians make 2027 demands
item.description: • Send strong messages to Tinubu, Atiku, Obi, Makinde, Adebayo, Donald Duke, others • Affordability, security, steady power supply top list By Steve Oko, Olasukanmi Akoni, Esther Onyegbula, Cynthia Alo, Shina Abubakar, Rotimi Ojomoyela, Golok Nanmwa, James Ogunnaike, Musa Ubandawaki, Peter Duru, Haruna Aliyu, Deola Badru & Chiamaka Ekwuwe Hunger is biting harder, insecurity is spreading fear across communities, businesses are groaning under the weight of rising energy costs, and millions of Nigerians are struggling to survive on incomes that can hardly meet their basic needs. From the farmer afraid of returning to his farm to the unemployed graduate searching endlessly for a job, the average Nigerian is looking towards the 2027 general elections, with 68 days to the polls, with one overriding expectation: a president who will make life worth living again. With the political atmosphere charged ahead of the presidential election, Nigerians across the country have sent a strong message to the presidential candidates: the next occupant of Aso Rock must move beyond campaign rhetoric and confront hunger, poverty, insecurity, unemployment, inflation and the worsening living conditions of citizens. Expectations The expectations are particularly high as President Bola Ahmed Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC) seeks another mandate, facing an array of contenders, including former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC); former Anambra State Governor, Peter Obi, of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC); Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM); Senator Sandy Ojang Onor of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP); former Cross River State Governor, Donald Duke, of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP); Omoyele Sowore of the African Action Congress (AAC); and Adewole Adebayo of the Social Democratic Party (SDP). item.content:encoded: • Send strong messages to Tinubu, Atiku, Obi, Makinde, Adebayo, Donald Duke, others • Affordability, security, steady power supply top list By Steve Oko, Olasukanmi Akoni, Esther Onyegbula, Cynthia Alo, Shina Abubakar, Rotimi Ojomoyela, Golok Nanmwa, James Ogunnaike, Musa Ubandawaki, Peter Duru, Haruna Aliyu, Deola Badru & Chiamaka Ekwuwe Hunger is biting harder, insecurity is spreading fear across communities, businesses are groaning under the weight of rising energy costs, and millions of Nigerians are struggling to survive on incomes that can hardly meet their basic needs. From the farmer afraid of returning to his farm to the unemployed graduate searching endlessly for a job, the average Nigerian is looking towards the 2027 general elections, with 68 days to the polls, with one overriding expectation: a president who will make life worth living again. Other candidates on the Independent National Electoral Commission’s published list include Sunday Chibuzo Okereke of the Labour Party (LP), Rufai Adekunle Omo-Aje of the Action Alliance (AA), Abbas-Bin Aliyu of the Action Democratic Party (ADP), Yusuf Kabiru of the Allied Peoples Party (APP), Sunday Adenuga of the Boot Party (BP), Moses Olusoji Adebisi of the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA), Ada Elizabeth Frederick Okwori of the National Democratic Party (NDP), Nkem Esther Okereke of the National Rescue Movement (NRM), Peter Ada Agada of the Young Progressives Party (YPP) and Daniel Daberechukwu Nwanyanwu of the Zenith Labour Party (ZLP). Survival Beyond the political parties, personalities and permutations surrounding the election, those who spoke to Sunday Vanguard in this public opinion survey said their concerns are fundamentally about survival, dignity and a better future. For some, the immediate concern is the price of food and petroleum products. For others, it is the frightening state of insecurity, unreliable electricity, unemployment and the deteriorating condition of public institutions. There are also those who believe that unless the electoral process, judiciary and other institutions are strengthened, successive administrations may continue to make promises without being held accountable. And in furtherance of this enthusiastic push for the significance of the civil service system as one critical cornerstone of democratic governance in Nigeria, CORFEPS has just launched an amazing initiative: the CORFEPS Journal on Pubic Policy and Governance. This significant initiative must be situated within a larger context of the institutional reform of the civil service system, especially its status as a value-based institution founded on merit, public spiritedness and professionalism. That context facilitates a framework that allows the past and the present to initiate conversation, and for both retired and current public servants to incessantly brainstorm the future of the bureaucratic system and its capability readiness to shoulder the burden of public policy implementation. The journal, I must say, presses the advantage of escalating the fundamental significance of professional knowledge and its role in deepening institutional progress. In other words, through it, CORFEPS provides a rare forum—draw, I dare say, from the administrative history of that golden era when administrative theorists (the gown) and practitioners (the town) were in conversation—within which administrative ideas, practices and initiatives could be discussed, extended and applied. The inaugural edition of the CORFEPS journal is indeed a full, rich and exciting package that is sufficiently exciting to signal to the communities of service and practice that something new and challenging has arrived in the administrative space. This is because the editorial board went all out to create a splash especially with the range of topics covered, and even more specially with the array of contributors and their unique specialties. As is to be expected, CORFEPS pulled strongly from within its own ranks for reflections that combine past administrative experiences with current observations from behind the scenes. The majority of the contributors are retired permanent secretaries who have served in one capacity or the other, and who have faced one crucial challenge or the other with wide ranging levels of successes. In this regard, the CORFEPS journal, in its inaugural edition, is drawing on the immense institutional memories and professional knowledge of its members to ventilate both diagnostic, recuperative and reformative insights. And this is salutary in ways that serve to complement the mediatory role CORFEPS has been playing as a staunch and energetic stakeholder in the civil service reform project in Nigeria. We now have an opportunity to listen and take note, outside of the usual high-power meetings, of the single-minded understanding of the civil service system from those who have manned its various aspects, especially the ministries, departments and agencies. Their reflections and analyses are complemented by others, critical watchers of the civil service, whose many years of dealing with the system make them significant participants in the ongoing efforts to transform it into a value-based, public-spirited, meritocratic and high-performing world class institution. The inaugural edition is divided into eight parts. Each of the segments, with the exception of the last two, speaks intentionally to the most dominant issues involved in assessing and transforming Nigeria’s democratic governance experiment. This is indeed a well-thought out scholarly first step by the editorial board. Part one, titled “The Nigerian Civil Service,” has four essays; part two with seven essays is concerned with governance tools; part three has just one essay dealing with Nigeria’s infrastructural development; part four has two essays surrounding leadership and management; the two essays in part five are wrapped around the theme of health and lifestyle; part six is dedicated to three book reviews; part seven signals recent appointments and tributes to distinguished former public servants; and part eight speaks to the activities of CORFEPS itself. In all, these thematic segments are all-encompassing. They are meant to lay on the table the diagnoses, prognoses and resolution frameworks for understanding the totality of Nigeria’s administrative and governance challenges and the ways forward to transcending them. His Vice President, JD Vance, was considerably more direct, declaring that “the reason we lost is the war.” That admission is particularly instructive. It establishes that the Republican defeat was not simply an abstract expression of public dissatisfaction with a sitting president. It was substantially connected to identifiable policy decisions and their consequences for American voters. The question, therefore, is why Nigeria’s opposition should expect the political consequences of Trump’s decision to engage Iran to automatically translate into an electoral liability for Tinubu. Nigeria did not initiate the conflict. Tinubu did not authorise American military operations against Iran. He does not determine American foreign policy, the direction of Trump’s trade tariffs or the domestic political calculations of the Republican Party. To suggest that the electoral consequences of these decisions constitute a direct verdict on Nigeria’s president is to stretch political analogy beyond its reasonable limits. Of course, the opposition is entitled to draw lessons from developments elsewhere. Political parties routinely study elections in other countries, particularly when they reveal the relationship between public expectations, government performance and electoral accountability. But learning from another country’s political experience is fundamentally different from assuming that its electoral outcome must be replicated elsewhere. There is an even more important distinction that deserves attention: the American midterm elections are not presidential elections. The midterms are held halfway through the president’s four-year tenure and determine the composition of Congress. They frequently become a referendum on the sitting president and his party, as voters use the opportunity to express satisfaction or dissatisfaction with the administration. Historically, the party controlling the White House has often faced considerable losses during midterm elections. Nigeria’s 2027 general election, by contrast, will be a presidential contest in which voters will choose the individual and political party they believe are best equipped to govern the country for another four years. The candidates will have to present their records, programmes, leadership credentials and policy alternatives before the Nigerian electorate. The difference is fundamental. A congressional election in the United States, influenced by a controversial foreign war, cannot automatically become a reliable predictor of a presidential election in Nigeria. But beyond the political comparison, there is a more substantive issue that Nigeria’s opposition must confront: the country’s economic circumstances and the choices available to any government seeking to address them. Structural weaknesses Nigeria’s economic difficulties did not begin on May 29, 2023. The country entered the Tinubu administration with longstanding structural weaknesses, including an expensive petrol subsidy regime, multiple exchange-rate arrangements, weak revenue mobilisation, infrastructure deficits, excessive dependence on imports and a productive sector constrained by years of economic distortions. These challenges accumulated over successive administrations and progressively reduced the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre. The new administration decided to confront some of these problems through the removal of petrol subsidy, foreign exchange reforms, fiscal restructuring and efforts to improve domestic revenue generation. These were not politically convenient decisions. Neither were they painless. Millions of Nigerians have experienced considerable hardship since the introduction of the reforms. The rising cost of food, transportation, electricity and other essential services has placed enormous pressure on households and businesses. No credible assessment of the Tinubu administration can ignore this reality, and no amount of economic statistics should be deployed to dismiss the daily struggles of ordinary citizens. However, the existence of hardship does not eliminate the need to examine the structural problems that necessitated reform in the first place. What would have happened if the government had continued to finance an increasingly expensive subsidy regime without addressing the distortions it created? What would have been the consequences of maintaining multiple exchange rates and the associated opportunities for arbitrage? Could Nigeria have continued accumulating fiscal liabilities while expecting its economy to become more competitive and attractive to investors? item.title: Countdown to 2027: Edo North is for Oshiomhole
item.description: By Allison Abanum Adams Oshiomhole’s first term has been defined by a deliberate strategy of translating legislative power into tangible federal presence for Edo North. As Chairman of the Senate Committee on Interior, he has leveraged his position to facilitate federal employment for constituents and ensure fair representation in federal institutions. His legislative record includes moving over 10 motions and sponsoring many bills. These are not abstract motions; they are institutional investments that will outlast any single political cycle. On the ground, Oshiomhole constituency interventions have reached all wards in Edo North, a coverage rate that speaks to both reach and intentionality. Oshiomhole has moved from delivering roads to delivering accountability, and Edo North have seen the difference in both bricks and budgets. Beyond infrastructure, his engagement with youth leaders and traditional rulers signals a recognition that representation must be relational, not transactional, a point underscored by his refusal to charge constituents for assistance and his warning against extortion in his name. The political consolidation around Oshiomhole 2027 bid reflects a broader strategic calculation within Edo North. Endorsements have since crossed traditional lines: From the market women in Auchi to the Artisan in Iyahmo, down to all the student bodies and community leaders, it is clear that it is no longer a question of whether Edo North is standing for Oshiomhole; it is a question of how loudly Edo North will say so. To the people in the rural areas of Edo North, they have risen from service, unity, and discipline: delivery that touches households, reconciliation that silences internal friction, and grassroots organisation that turns intention into votes. The good people of Edo North on their own are moving ward by ward to get support for Oshiomhole. The plough is heavy; the hands must be steady because the furrow ahead is 2027. The message is clear: no retreat, no sideways glance, no nostalgia for old battles in Edo North. A senatorial district that has seen the light and future must now prove it can cultivate it, row by row, ward by ward, state by state, until the harvest of triumph is achieved. Every leader, every member, every supporter keeps eyes on the furrow, not on the noise. So, let the word go forth: APC is on the plough, and there is no looking back until Oshiomhole is sent back to the Senate in 2027. The task is not to boast of yesterday but to labour for tomorrow with humility, focus, and determination. The harvest belongs to those who keep ploughing. For a senatorial district that has historically oscillated between alignment and agitation, the emerging consensus is that Oshiomhole federal network is an asset too valuable to surrender. Without gas lighting, these political highflyers’ ‘selling points’ make any of them eminently qualified to represent the Anioma nationality in the Red Chamber. However, one knows that making a choice out of these two top contenders, especially by voters in a dynamic and highly unpredictable democratic space like ours where selfish and primordial sentiments hold sway, is certainly a herculean task, yet a candidate’s ‘report card’ remains an added advantage. For Okowa, he is majorly regarded as a grassroots politician who walks his talk in terms of mass mobilisation, especially across the nine councils that make up the Delta North Senatorial District. Evidently too, the former governor’s enduring stay in the political trenches for over three decades tells a reassuring story of one who understands the undercurrents and dynamics of power ‘capture’. Moreover, Okowa has other political assets to take to the electioneering field; he has a vast and extensive experience in the executive and the legislative arms of government, and no matter how hard his traducers knock him, he being an ex -state executive, has a chunk of tangible and verifiable score cards to present to his Delta North constituents. As the campaigns intensify, he will readily reel out the dividends of democracy he provided as a sitting governor to his Delta North voters. Even his consultative town hall meetings have been turned into endorsements of sorts by traditional institutions -though an exercise dismissed by Ochei’s camp as a mere smokescreen in a democratic dispensation anchored on one man, one vote mantra. Moreover, for a political strongman believed largely to be an ‘Establishment’ candidate, Okowa would be waging a double barreled war against his contenders, as he will leverage not only on the state government’s mobilisation drive, but most likely as well as from its near inelastic financial muscle. Truth is: Okowa’s opponents must be ready to deepen their resource base to be able to match him in the battle royale for the exalted Abuja seat. At this juncture, therefore, one is tempted to ask: Are Okowa’s intimidating credentials and robust service- delivery profile over the years enough pointers to cow any of his opponents to throw in the towel and make a cautious and timely retreat from the political battle field. In other words, can Ochei, a major contender, continue to tackle a man who has withered various political storms, tempest and near deadly intrigues? Well, feelers one gets from those who know Ochei closely say, he is not one who easily runs away from political battles, many others describe him as a human dynamo and an incurable optimist who dares where even angels thread softly. Moreover, he is coming to the electioneering arena with a dose of youthful dynamism and vibrancy. At 57, Ochei is believed to leverage on his mass appeal among the youths, as his message of generational shift in leadership resonates far and wide in the nine councils of Delta North. He and his teeming supporters are already taking a swipe at Okowa for allegedly foisting a clandestine political dynasty for his family and cronies. Still, Ochei who flaunts his impressive performance as a former lawmaker for Aniocha North echoes that his mission to the Senate is to replicate that same feat in the entire Delta North, insisting he has the capacity and political sagacity to attract federal presence to Anioma land more than any other candidate. Ochei and his supporters are equally taking his redemptive message to town, affirming that he is on a rescue mission, to bridge what they call the ‘huge infrastructural decay’ in Delta North despite the zone’s role in the electoral victory of the now APC -led administration in the State. In his resolute bid to actualise his vision at the Senate if elected, Ochei has rolled out a 10 -point Agenda encapsulated in an all- inclusive governance, better security, power, job opportunities, infrastructure, agriculture, productivity, among others. Also, the former Speaker is latching onto the integrity and impeccable qualities of his party’s Presidential candidate, Mr. Peter Obi, to drive his message of redemption home. Moreover, the NDC flag bearer is making much capital from what he regards as the ‘suffocating hardship’ in the country occasioned by the removal of fuel subsidy by the APC- led federal government ,to market his candidacy. Well, as the January 16, 2027 polls draws nearer, the most pertinent questions on many lips are: Between Okowa and Ochei, who blinks first? Can Ochei, a candidate described by Okowa’s many supporters as a feather weight, pull a surprise, and possibly upstage the steely ex-governor in the electoral contest? Or will the enigmatic Okowa clinch the coveted Senate seat seamlessly? Well, let’s not beat our chest in certainty as to which direction the political pendulum will swing towards, after all the projections and permutations here are mere conjectures buried in the womb of time. •Nwagboniwe, a journalist, writes from Lagos. item.title: FG plans National Sports Commission office in Kwara – Magaji
item.description: By Demola Akinyemi ILORIN – The Federal Government has concluded plans to establish an office of the National Sports Commission (NSC) in Kwara State, following the development of sports facilities by the administration of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq. The Executive Chairman of the Kwara State Sports Commission, Coach Bola Magaji, disclosed this in Ilorin, saying officials of the NSC had been impressed by the facilities provided by the state government. Magaji spoke at the unveiling of a book titled The Sardauna of Ilorin in the Eyes of History, written in honour of AbdulRazaq, who holds the traditional title of Sardauna of Ilorin. The book was authored by Abiodun Abdul Kareem, a senior journalist and editor of Herald on Sunday, the Sunday publication of the Kwara State Printing and Publishing Corporation. Magaji recalled that officials of the National Sports Commission visited Kwara about three weeks ago to assess the sports facilities developed by the AbdulRazaq administration over the past seven years. He said the officials expressed satisfaction with the facilities at the state stadium complex and indicated that the proposed NSC office would be established in the state. According to him, the development reflects the growing recognition of Kwara’s investment in sports infrastructure. Magaji said the state’s stadium complex could boast of some of the best squash court facilities in the world, adding that Kwara contingents to national and international sporting competitions had recorded improved medal-winning performances. He attributed the development to investments in sports infrastructure and efforts to promote sporting activities in the state. Also speaking, the Special Adviser and Counsellor to the Governor, Alhaji Saad Salahudeen, said AbdulRazaq’s contributions to governance, politics, youth development and national development would continue to attract attention in the years ahead. He said the governor’s footprints in public service would remain relevant and be referenced in the next 50 years. Earlier, the Chairman of the Organising Committee, Mallam Umar Abdulwahab, said the event was designed to provide a platform for discussions on leadership, public service, governance and historical preservation. He said the initiative was also aimed at documenting experiences and inspiring future generations. The event was attended by several dignitaries, including the Emir of Ilorin, Alhaji Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, who was represented by Magaji Ogundele; Alhaji Saad Kajola; Alhaji Yusuf Abdullahi; the Secretary to the State Government, Professor Mamman Jibril; Senior Adviser on Islamic Religion, Alhaji Ibrahim Danmegoro; and Senior Adviser on Political Communication, Alhaji Bashir Adigun, among others. He argued that his legislative experience had given him a broad understanding of governance, particularly through the House of Assembly’s appropriation and oversight responsibilities, which he said complemented the executive’s implementation of policies and projects. The governorship candidate, an electrical engineering graduate, also highlighted his academic pursuits, disclosing that he had undertaken programmes in revenue management, peace, conflict and security studies and was currently pursuing a PhD in economic development. Reflecting on his representation of Ilesha/Gwanara Constituency, Danladi identified access to potable water, rural roads, healthcare, education and security as some of the major challenges that informed his legislative interventions. He said he facilitated the provision of about 210 boreholes across communities in his constituency during his first term, alongside the construction and rehabilitation of rural roads. One of the projects he highlighted was a 33-kilometre road linking communities in the constituency, which he said had significantly improved movement in the area. According to him, residents previously endured several hours of travelling during the rainy season for journeys that would ordinarily take about 30 minutes. On healthcare, the Speaker said he facilitated interventions in 18 primary healthcare centres and supported efforts to improve existing general and cottage hospitals. He added that his interventions had extended beyond his constituency, noting that his position as Speaker had provided opportunities to support development projects and empowerment programmes in other parts of the state. Addressing insecurity, particularly in Kwara North, Danladi said he facilitated the training of 300 local security personnel to strengthen surveillance and intelligence gathering in vulnerable communities, especially border settlements in Baruten Local Government Area. He described security as fundamental to development and called for sustained collaboration among security agencies, traditional rulers, community leaders and local authorities. On his proposed administration’s priorities, the APC candidate listed human capital development, agriculture, electricity and rural infrastructure as key areas of focus. He said improved road networks connecting farming communities to urban markets would reduce transportation costs, increase farmers’ earnings and contribute to lower food prices. Danladi also lamented electricity challenges confronting several rural communities in Baruten, but said partnerships with investors had facilitated alternative power arrangements, including solar-powered electricity in some settlements. He identified the establishment of the Federal Science and Technical College in Kwara North as another important intervention capable of expanding educational opportunities and stimulating development in the district. On the political debate surrounding calls to rescue Kwara, the APC candidate questioned the rationale behind such demands, arguing that the state should focus on consolidating its development efforts. “Why are some people saying they want to rescue Kwara? Is it from the infrastructure and development that are going on, or do we want to move forward? In life, there is no limit to development. We must continue to move forward,” he said. He described AbdulRazaq as a leader who had laid a foundation for the state’s development, pledging to sustain ongoing programmes and improve on existing achievements. “My brother has laid a good foundation for Kwara, and the next step is for us to build on that foundation. I am part and parcel of the foundation. It will therefore be easier for us to consolidate the gains already recorded,” he said. Danladi also pledged balanced development across the three senatorial districts, assuring residents of Kwara North, Central and South that none would be neglected under his administration. He expressed optimism about the economic potential of Kwara North, particularly in agriculture, rural infrastructure and electricity, saying strategic investments in the areas would stimulate economic activities and discourage rural-urban migration.
